clue.text: Various crimes associated with soldier, a criminal

indicators.note: Calling the crimes various says they come in no settled form, and letters with no settled form are letters waiting to be reordered.

parts.note: six letters handed straight over from the clue for reordering
ant colonies keep a soldier caste, so setters use soldier for the insect

explanation.surface: Assorted offences being pinned on a serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: A soldier here is an ant: colonies really do have a soldier caste, and setters lean on that sense whenever an army turns up in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: a criminal → MISCREANT: a plain synonym for a wrongdoer, carrying a faintly old-fashioned, disapproving edge that 'criminal' on its own lacks.

clue.text: I'm twice upset about impersonator

indicators.note: In a down clue upset means tipped over end to end, so the letters just built are read from the bottom upwards.
Doing something twice means writing it out a second time, so the two letters before this word are set down again.

parts.note: I'M as its two letters, then the same two letters again
c is short for circa, about, as used before an uncertain date

explanation.surface: The speaker is rattled at being quoted back at themselves twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset about' reads as one phrase describing a mood, and the two words are separate jobs; c for circa is the small piece hiding at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: impersonator → MIMIC: a mimic copies another person's voice and manner, which is what an impersonator does for a living.

clue.text: Trustworthy from the period of religious education

parts.note: since means from the time that, covering a stretch running up to now
RE is what British school timetables call religious education

explanation.surface: Dependability dating back to somebody's schooldays in religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Period' is doing double duty: a lesson on the school timetable in the surface, and a stretch of time in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Trustworthy → SINCERE: sincere means genuine in what you say and feel, and somebody who means what they say is somebody you can trust.

clue.text: Travel widely — Italy's capital, we hear

indicators.note: What you hear is the noise a word makes, so the grid takes the sound of the place named rather than its spelling.

parts.note: the capital city of Italy is Rome, and said aloud it comes out on the page with different vowels

explanation.surface: Travel advice, with the Italian capital held up as the place to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italy's capital' wants to be the letter I, the capital letter the country's name starts with, and it is the city instead — said out loud, not spelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel widely → ROAM: to roam is to wander with no fixed route, covering ground for its own sake rather than heading anywhere.

clue.text: Desert-like? Help to bring in river

indicators.note: Bringing something in carries it indoors, so the letter named next is placed inside the word before it.

parts.note: aid is help, as noun and as verb
r is the map-maker's abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Relief supplies being brought in along a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by comparison rather than a synonym: nothing here is a desert, only like one.
explanation.definitionFit: Desert-like? → ARID: arid means so dry that nothing will grow, which is exactly the quality that makes a desert a desert.

clue.text: Excellent access to concert? O, boy, excited

indicators.note: Something excited will not sit still, and letters that will not sit still come out in an order other than the printed one.

parts.note: a ticket is what gets you in at the door of a concert
the four letters of O and BOY stirred into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Sheer delight at landing a seat for the concert.
explanation.walkthrough: TICKETY-BOO is dated British slang for everything running smoothly — the sort of thing a 1940s film pilot says over the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent → TICKETY-BOO: British slang for a situation that is in perfect order, said of how things are going rather than of a thing.

clue.text: Recalled very old Southern French artist

indicators.note: To recall is to call something back, and in an across clue calling letters back reads them from right to left.

parts.note: somebody very old is aged
S is the compass abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: A painter from the south being remembered in his old age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' reads as remembered in a sentence about an elderly painter, and it is an instruction instead. Impressionists are the setter's favourite artists to clue.
explanation.definitionFit: French artist → DEGAS: Edgar Degas, the Impressionist of the ballet dancers — a definition by example, one painter standing for the category.

clue.text: Floral arrangement is presented within 24 hours — church gets one in

indicators.note: To be presented within something is to be handed over inside it, so those two letters land in the middle of the word that follows.

parts.note: a day is the 24 hours the clock takes to come round
the word itself, dropped in unchanged
CH is the standard short form of church, as printed on maps
a stands in for one, as in a hundred pounds
the word again taken at face value, two letters as they stand

explanation.surface: Flowers delivered inside a day, with the church getting a bunch as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves hand you words to use exactly as printed — the tiny 'is' and 'in' contribute their own letters, which is easy to miss while hunting for a mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: Floral arrangement → DAISY CHAIN: the string of daisies children thread together, an arrangement of flowers in the most literal and least florist sense.

clue.text: Source of mischief? Grand rock band getting nothing back

parts.note: g is the standard short form of grand
REM were the American rock band of Losing My Religion

indicators.note: Sending a word back turns it round, so the three letters just named are written out in the opposite order.

parts.note: nil is nothing, the word used for a score of none

explanation.surface: A big-name band who get nothing in return for their trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: GREMLINs were invented by RAF pilots in the 1920s: the imps that sabotage an aircraft, which is why a machine failing for no reason still has one.
explanation.definitionFit: Source of mischief? → GREMLIN: the imaginary imp blamed when machinery misbehaves, so it names the cause of the trouble rather than the trouble.

clue.text: Quickly call major player and face receiving bit of pushback

indicators.note: A word that receives something takes it in, so the letter named next lands inside the piece before it.
A bit of a word is not the whole of it, and the bit a setter means by default is the letter it opens with.

parts.note: a seed is a ranked player kept apart in the draw at a major tournament
the first letter of the word
the dial is the face of a clock or a gauge

explanation.surface: Ringing a star player who is meeting a little resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' is the trap: it looks like the verb, one player facing another, and it is the noun — the face a pair of hands go round.
explanation.definitionFit: Quickly call → SPEED-DIAL: to speed-dial somebody is to ring them off a single stored key, calling faster than dialling the number out.

clue.text: Small orange feature, see, represented in an Asian language

indicators.note: Read as re-presented, the word means shown again in a fresh arrangement, which is what happens to the three letters before it.

parts.note: a mandarin is the small loose-skinned orange
the chin is a feature of the face
the three letters of SEE set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A small citrus fruit, apparently, drawn with its parts labelled in a foreign tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Small orange' as two adjectives describing the feature; it is a noun standing alone, the fruit itself.
explanation.definitionFit: an Asian language → MANDARIN CHINESE: the standard form of Chinese spoken across most of China, so it names one particular Asian language.

clue.text: Team boasted

definitions.meaning: the group who work a boat, a shift or a film set together
the past tense of crow, which is what a cockerel and a winner both do

explanation.surface: A sports side bragging about the result.
explanation.walkthrough: The past tense of crow survives now almost only in 'the cock crew', which is why the second half of this clue reads as a different word altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: Team → CREW: the people who work a boat or a shift together; and boasted → CREW, the archaic past tense of crow, and to crow is to boast.

clue.text: Type of transport in Post Office colour given a second chance?

indicators.note: The little word puts one thing inside another, so the transport named before it goes within the colour named after it.

parts.note: British post boxes and Royal Mail vans are red, the Post Office's own livery
a cycle is a way of getting about

explanation.surface: Some form of transport turning up in postal red.
explanation.walkthrough: Pillar-box red is the colour of British post boxes and Royal Mail vans — a shade a whole country knows by the Post Office's name.
explanation.definitionFit: given a second chance? → RECYCLED: material that has been used, reclaimed and put back into service, which is a second chance in the physical sense.

clue.text: Thrilling tale from assistant to pianist

definitions.meaning: a story so gripping that you keep going to the next page
the person who sits at the keyboard's left and turns the score at the right bar

explanation.surface: A gripping story coming from the person sitting beside the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a real job: at a recital somebody sits beside the pianist and turns the sheet music at exactly the right bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrilling tale → PAGE-TURNER: a book so gripping you keep turning pages; and assistant to pianist → the person who literally turns the pages of the score.

clue.text: Breakdown of insect, if I start to consider like an entomologist?

indicators.note: A breakdown takes a thing apart into its components, and components can be put back together in any order.

parts.note: nine letters handed over to be rearranged

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it begins with, so only that opening letter joins the mixture.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bug specialist beginning to take a specimen apart.
explanation.walkthrough: An entomologist is an insect scientist, so the letters being shuffled and the definition describe the same person's working day and the seam between them barely shows.
explanation.definitionFit: like an entomologist? → SCIENTIFIC: an entomologist is a scientist, so proceeding like one is proceeding scientifically; the question mark flags the definition by example.

clue.text: People in power greeting revival of archery

definitions.note: The definition is plural and names the individuals, while the answer is singular and names the ranked structure they make up — a collective noun standing for the group.

indicators.note: A revival brings something back in a new form, and letters brought back in a new form are letters reordered.

parts.note: hi is the everyday greeting
the seven letters of the sport rearranged

explanation.surface: A warm welcome given to the comeback of the bow and arrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revival of archery' reads as a news story about a sport coming back into fashion, and the word 'revival' is the setter's instruction hiding inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: People in power → HIERARCHY: the ranked order of authority in an organisation, used loosely for the set of people occupying its top ranks.

clue.text: A measure of time for us tucking into hot drink container

indicators.note: To tuck into something is to get right inside it, so the letters named before end up in among what comes after.

parts.note: H is the letter on the hot tap
what belongs to us is our, the possessive of the same pronoun
a glass is what a drink is served in

explanation.surface: Something poured out for us into a hot-drink flask.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot drink container' wants to be one object, a mug or a thermos, and it splits: the hot is a single letter, and the container is what a cold drink comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure of time → HOURGLASS: the twin-bulbed glass whose sand runs through in a fixed span, so the object itself measures out a period.

clue.text: Starts to herald a new operation in Vietnamese city

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it begins with, and the plural says to take one from each of the words that follow.

parts.note: the first letter of the word
a one-letter word, so its opening letter is all of it
the initial of the word
the first letter of the word
the initial of the last word in the run

explanation.surface: The announcement of a new military campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Five words in a row give up their opening letters, and 'in' is one of them — the small linking words are exactly where a solver stops looking.
explanation.definitionFit: Vietnamese city → HANOI: the capital of Vietnam, up in the north of the country; a definition by example, since the country has other cities.

clue.text: A long time in pursuit of American custom

indicators.note: Whatever is in pursuit of something follows along behind it, so the letters named first are written after the ones named next.

parts.note: US is the standard short form of the country, so it covers American
an age is a long stretch of time

explanation.surface: Somebody chasing an American habit for years on end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A long time' opens the clue where a definition usually sits and is wordplay instead; the definition is the single word left at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: custom → USAGE: usage is established practice, the way a thing has come to be done, which is what a custom is once it settles.

clue.text: Researcher etching a line in any stone

indicators.note: To etch is to cut a mark into a surface, so the letters named next are set down inside the word that follows.

parts.note: the word as it stands, prised open to take the insertion
the single letter, used literally
l is the abbreviation for line, as in a page-and-line reference
st is the British abbreviation for the stone, the fourteen-pound unit of body weight

explanation.surface: Somebody scratching a line into a piece of rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Any' looks like a vague adjective attached to the stone, and it is a whole word to be prised apart — the plainest words in the clue are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Researcher → ANALYST: an analyst is paid to take data apart and report what it shows, which is research in the commercial and intelligence sense.

clue.text: Energy proposal for conference almost entirely affected by feelings

indicators.note: Almost means falling just short, so the word it governs arrives with its final letter missing.

parts.note: E is the physicist's symbol for energy
a motion is the proposal put before a conference for debate
ALL means entirely, and it turns up here one letter short

explanation.surface: An energy proposal going to conference, very nearly complete.
explanation.walkthrough: Deletion clues hang on a word you have to supply first: 'entirely' is not describing anything here, it is the word ALL waiting to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: affected by feelings → EMOTIONAL: the adjective for a person governed by their feelings rather than their judgement, or a scene charged with them.

clue.text: No source of coal linked to European candidate

parts.note: the word taken as it stands
coal is dug out of a mine
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European put forward despite having no coal behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of' almost always asks for a first letter, and here it means what it says: the place the coal comes out of.
explanation.definitionFit: candidate → NOMINEE: a nominee is the person formally put forward for a post or a prize, which is what standing as a candidate amounts to.

clue.text: BA or MA? DA, GA, true, would be wrong

definitions.note: BA and MA name the degrees, while the answer is the person holding one; the question mark is the setter admitting the definition works by example rather than by synonym.

indicators.note: Something written wrong has its letters out of place, so the pieces listed before this are not yet in the order the grid wants.

parts.note: eight letters offered as two pairs and a word, to be reordered

explanation.surface: Somebody reeling off degree abbreviations and getting them muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a run of two-letter pairs, so the eye takes the whole line as one list and never notices that only the first two belong to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: BA or MA? → GRADUATE: both are university degrees, and whoever has been awarded one has by definition graduated.

clue.text: In the morning the writer returned a classic novel

indicators.note: To return something is to send it back the way it came, and in an across clue that means reading the letters right to left.

parts.note: am marks the hours before noon on a clock
the writer of the clue is the setter, referring to himself

explanation.surface: An early call from the author, bringing a borrowed book back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter talking about himself, a convention worth owning: when a clue mentions the author, the writer or yours truly, it usually wants ME or I.
explanation.definitionFit: a classic novel → EMMA: Jane Austen's 1815 novel of a matchmaker who gets everything wrong — one named classic standing in for the category.

clue.text: Something useful when fixed

parts.note: as can replace when: as I arrived, when I arrived
something set is fixed, like a set time or a jelly that has set

explanation.surface: Something that comes in handy once it has been mended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When fixed' reads as a condition — useful only after repair — and both of its words are separate synonyms to be laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something useful → ASSET: anything of value working in your favour, from an item on a balance sheet to a helpful person on the team.

clue.text: Crag's lowest edge is dark and gloomy

indicators.note: In a down clue the lowest letter of a word is the one at its end, so the final letter of the word before is all that is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of the word, sitting at its foot in a down clue
the rim is the edge of a cup or a wheel

explanation.surface: The bottom lip of a rock face looking bleak.
explanation.walkthrough: Down clues can point at a letter by its height on the page, so 'lowest' is not describing the crag but picking the letter at the bottom of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: dark and gloomy → GRIM: grim describes a scene that is bleak and forbidding, the mood of a dark, gloomy place rather than its light level.

clue.text: A cuppa with the first of my co-workers?

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: a team is one body made of many people, and the question mark covers the switch from the members to the group they form.

parts.note: a cuppa is British for a cup of tea, and almost never means coffee

indicators.note: The first of a word is the letter it opens with, so a single letter comes across from what follows.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Sharing a brew with the people you work alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is carrying the weight: the clue names the individuals and the grid wants the single word for the body they add up to.
explanation.definitionFit: co-workers? → TEAM: a team is the group of people who work together on something, so it names the colleagues collectively rather than one by one.

clue.text: Theatrical encouragement to play in afternoon? Yes, possibly involving any number

indicators.note: Saying a thing is possibly so admits it is not so as printed, and letters not as printed are letters to be reordered.
What is involved is drawn into the business at hand, so the letter named after this word joins the pool being rearranged.

parts.note: fourteen letters offered up to be rearranged
n is the mathematician's letter for an unspecified number

explanation.surface: An afternoon game being agreed to, with the numbers still to be settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyone for tennis?' is the stock line of drawing-room comedy — the cheerful young man arriving through the French windows with a racquet — which is what makes it theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical encouragement to play → ANYONE FOR TENNIS: the catchphrase entrance line of 1920s drawing-room drama, an invitation to come out and play a game.

clue.text: Top performer adopting one Indian instrument

indicators.note: A family adopting a child takes them in as their own, so the letter named next is taken inside the word before it.

parts.note: the top performer on the bill is the star
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A leading act taking up an unfamiliar instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The SITAR is the long-necked Indian lute Ravi Shankar played, and the 'one' inside it arrives as a Roman numeral rather than as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian instrument → SITAR: the long-necked, many-stringed lute of Indian classical music — a definition by example, one instrument standing for the class.

clue.text: Pet going round leg, perhaps, to get cheese

indicators.note: Something going round another thing wraps itself about it, so the word before is split to sit either side of what follows.

parts.note: the household pet a setter reaches for first
a member is a limb, and a leg is one instance of one — hence the 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: A cat winding itself round somebody's leg by the fridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' for a limb is an old sense kept alive largely by crosswords, and 'perhaps' is the flag that a leg is only one example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: cheese → CAMEMBERT: the soft, bloomy-rinded cheese from Normandy — a definition by example, one named cheese standing for the whole class.
